sections.title: What is somatic self-regulation, in one sentence?
Is somatic self-regulation the same as somatic therapy?
How long does it take to work?
Is this the same as the vagus nerve reset?

blocks.p: Somatic self-regulation is the ongoing, body-based practice of returning your nervous system to a state of safety and connection, through your own attention, breath, and movement.

"Somatic" just means "of the body." "Self-regulation" means you are the one doing the returning. Together, they describe something most of us were never taught: how to notice what's happening inside your body and gently guide it back toward connection.

That's the definition. But I want to be careful with it, because the word regulation has gotten loud online lately. It's been dressed up in marketing. It's been handed over to protocols, resets, and seven-day challenges. And that's not what this is.

Let me say this plainly as a licensed therapist who works with this every day: somatic self-regulation is not a hack. It is not a trick. It is not a thing you unlock. It is a practice, simple, small, daily, and uniquely yours.
You already have a nervous system that knows how to regulate. Your job is to practice getting out of its way and giving it what it needs.

Before I share the three simple, foundational skills that form the bedrock of this work, we need to understand what this practice isn't. If you've been searching online for help with anxiety, freeze, trauma, or just feeling chronically "off," you've probably encountered a landscape that looks like this:

ul: "Reset your vagus nerve in 7 days." You can't. The vagus nerve isn't broken. It doesn't need resetting. The framing is wrong.
"The one exercise that will change your nervous system." There isn't one. Anyone selling a single exercise as a solution is selling nonsensical false hope, not regulation.
"Hack your polyvagal state." Polyvagal states are not computers. They are not code. They are the body's response to the felt sense of safety or danger. You don't hack them; you relate to them.

"Cold plunge your way to calm." Extreme physiological interventions, such as ice baths, breath-holding protocols, and vibration devices, can produce short-term state shifts. They also bypass the slow, relational work your nervous system needs. I'm not saying never. I'm saying: this is not the foundation… and you'll likely be left disappointed.
"The somatic technique therapists don't want you to know." Therapists absolutely want you to know. We want you to know everything. The ones you see on TikTok and the ones you don't.

blocks.p: The thing they all have in common is the promise of speed. Of a shortcut. Of completion.
Somatic self-regulation is the opposite of that. It is slow, ongoing, and it gets easier the longer you do it, but it never stops being a practice. (That's the part most marketing leaves out.)
Somatic self-regulation has three parts:

ol: Somatic: rooted in the body, not the cognitive story about the body.
Self: you are the agent. Not a device, not a protocol, not a therapist doing it to you.
Regulation: movement back toward presence and connection; inherently a biological process toward homeostasis.

blocks.p: Regulation is not the same as relaxation. It is not the same as calm. A regulated nervous system can be activated (excited, focused, mobilized) and still be regulated, as long as that activation is appropriate to what's happening and can come back down when the moment passes.

The opposite of regulation isn't stress; it's being stuck. Stuck in a mobilized state (chronic anxiety, hypervigilance). Stuck in an immobilized one (shutdown, numbness, collapse). Somatic self-regulation is the practice of gradually getting unstuck.
You're not broken. You're stuck. (Hence the name of my podcast, Stuck Not Broken.)

Somatic self-regulation makes the most sense when you understand a little about how the autonomic nervous system actually works. This is where Polyvagal Theory comes in. I'll keep it brief here as I have numerous deep-dive explainers (like my [Polyvagal Intro](piece:snb101-polyvagal-101-foundations)), but the short version is:
Your autonomic nervous system can be in three primary states.

ul: Ventral vagal: connected, present, safe. You can think clearly, feel your emotions without overwhelm, and relate to others with empathy. [More about safety](hub:safety)
Sympathetic: mobilized. Fight, flight, urgency, anxiety. Needed at times, but a problem when you're stuck there. [More about flight/fight](hub:fightflight)
Dorsal vagal: immobilized. Shutdown, collapse, numbness. Also needed at times, and also a problem when you're stuck there. [More about shutdown](hub:shutdown)

blocks.p: Your nervous system moves through these states all day. That's normal. Regulation isn't about staying in Ventral Vagal all the time. It's about being able to return to it after you leave.
Returning to ventral vagal safety is essential to somatic self-regulation practices.

blocks.h: A foundational practice: three somatic skills

blocks.p: This isn't a rigid protocol or a hack. These are three fundamental skills to practice. They are the 'how' behind developing a real relationship with your nervous system. They are the beginning of working somatically.

ul: What it is: Using your senses to connect to your immediate environment. This is the first step, using simple mindfulness to open the potential to journey inward.

How to practice: Use your senses and simply notice what they're picking up. Don't control it. This isn't the 5-4-3-2-1 method. To orient mindfully, just notice what your senses are drawn toward, like the silence in the room or the view out your window.
Why it works: This simple mindfulness practice can instantly lead to more stillness and present-moment connection. This is the foundation.
What it is: Using your conscious awareness to pay attention to your body's natural breathing rhythm without trying to change it.
How to practice: Just pay attention to your breathing. Don't control it. We work with what is true in the present moment.

Why it works: Your body knows how to breathe. Often, when you simply pay attention to your natural breathing, your body spontaneously shifts its own pattern, perhaps from chest to belly or from tense to relaxed. The breath is a gateway to your internal world.
What it is: Validating the emotions you feel. Aligning your thoughts with your somatic experiences.
How to practice: After connecting to the external world and your breath, tell the truth about your emotions. Just fill in the blank: "I feel _."

Why it works: Self-regulation can't happen if your conscious mind is at war with your body's experience. If you feel anxious, your mind needs to acknowledge that. Compare the two: "I feel anxious, and it makes sense why I do." Or: "I don't want to feel anxious. How can I make this go away!?"

blocks.prompt: Fill in the blank, honestly: "I feel ____."

blocks.p: Change happens over time. Small practices in small doses lead to significant, sustainable changes.

blocks.why: Orienting to what's around you, your natural breath, and an honest "I feel": the three skills, tuned to you.

blocks.h: How to start: the smallest possible practice

blocks.p: If you take one thing from this post, take this: start with 30 seconds, once a day.

Not thirty minutes. Not an app. Not a workshop. Thirty seconds of one of the three skills above. Pick whichever one feels easiest. Do it at a consistent time, after you wake up, before you eat lunch, or when you close your laptop. If 30 seconds feels too small, that means there's no mental friction to stop you.
I think many people "fail" at nervous system practice not because of willpower, but because of unrealistic expectations. Build a sustainable practice:

ul: Weeks 1 to 2: Thirty seconds a day, same skill, same time. Miss a day? Restart without shame the next day.
Weeks 3 to 6: Two minutes a day. Add a second skill if you want, or go deeper with one.
Weeks 7 onward: Three to five minutes a day, spread out as small moments. Orient before meetings. Check your breath in line at the grocery store.

blocks.p: This is a sustainable practice that pays off over time.

blocks.h: What to do next: deeper, structured practices

blocks.p: Once you are comfortable with these foundational skills, you can expand on them. A lot. This is where we move from simple, in-the-moment skills to a more structured, nuanced protocol for getting unstuck.

A deeper practice involves acknowledging your emotion, normalizing it, giving it permission to be there, feeling it in your body at the level of sensation (heat, tension, etc.), and then mindfully following the impulse that arises.

If that sounds like a lot, it is! It takes patience and a firm anchoring in your [Ventral Vagal safety state](piece:polyvagal-safety). This deeper, systematic work is what I teach inside my structured programs. The foundational skills in this article are the prerequisites.
The knowledge and practices for this next level are streamlined in my most comprehensive resources:

ul: The Unstucking Academy: Students follow the [Unstucking Pathway](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) and use pre-recorded guided practices.

The Stuck Not Broken books: [These three books](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/books) teach you the theory, help strengthen your safety state, and guide you in getting unstuck on a deep, somatic level.

blocks.h: Common obstacles (and what to do with them)

blocks.p: "I can't feel my body." This likely means the nervous system is in a protective state, where interoception, the felt awareness of internal sensations, has dialed down. Start with external orienting and connecting with your natural breath, not with an internal sensation. Internal awareness comes much later.

"It makes me feel worse." Somatic practice can bring up what's been held. If a practice consistently dysregulates you, stop that practice and try a different one. Orienting and breath connection are the gentlest starting places. Avoid deep breath work, meditation, and internal scanning if they reliably take you into distress. This is especially important if you have a trauma history. A body-based therapist can help you find entry points that work for your system.
"I keep forgetting." Attach the practice to something you already do reliably, like a morning coffee. Make it as small and simple as possible.

"I don't feel anything different." You won't, at first, and you may not for weeks. Regulation doesn't announce itself. You'll notice it by proxy, you reacted less to something that usually sets you off, or you noticed your shoulders were tight and let them drop without deciding to. That's the practice working. It is not dramatic, but over time, it's noticeable.

"Isn't this just mindfulness?" Mindfulness and somatic self-regulation overlap significantly, and both are useful. The difference is emphasis. Mindfulness often centers awareness. Somatic work centers the body's response to that awareness, what shifts, what settles, what doesn't. In practice, you'll use both.
Somatic self-regulation is powerful. It is also not the answer to everything.

If you are dealing with chronic dysregulation rooted in trauma, childhood adversity, acute traumatic events, ongoing relational harm, a daily practice alone is usually not sufficient. You need literal external safety and maybe what the polyvagal world calls co-regulation: the experience of your nervous system settling in the presence of another regulated nervous system.
Co-regulation is what happens in good therapy. It is also what happens in good friendships, good partnerships, and a safe community.

Co-regulation is not a failure of self-regulation. It is the foundation of it. Human nervous systems were never meant to regulate alone. Solo practice gives you capacity; a relationship gives you the ground on which that capacity rests.

If you are in sustained dysregulation, panic that won't quit, shutdown that won't lift, numbness that feels like drowning, please seek support. A somatic therapist (SEP, sensorimotor, polyvagal-informed) can help you find practices that fit your nervous system and can provide the [co-regulation](hub:rel) that solo practice cannot.

If you're not sure whether what you're experiencing is shutdown specifically, start with the full explanation: [Dorsal Vagal Shutdown: Signals, Symptoms & How to Come Out of It](piece:dorsal-vagal-shutdown)
It is worth saying plainly, once: the nervous system space online is noisy, and a lot of it is selling you something. Resets. Protocols. Devices. Seven-day transformations.

I understand the appeal. I also know that the people I work with who make the most durable changes are the ones who give up the search for shortcuts and pick a small practice they can do tomorrow and the day after that.
If what you find on Stuck Not Broken feels less flashy than the rest of the internet, that's on purpose. Daily practice is less flashy than hacks. It also works.

blocks.h3: What is somatic self-regulation, in one sentence?

blocks.p: It's the ongoing, body-based practice of returning your nervous system to a place of safety, connection, and presence, using attention, breath, and movement rather than protocols or external interventions.

blocks.h3: Is somatic self-regulation the same as somatic therapy?

blocks.p: No. Somatic therapy is a professional modality (Somatic Experiencing, Sensorimotor Psychotherapy, Polyvagal-informed therapy) delivered by a trained clinician. Somatic self-regulation is the daily practice you can do on your own, often alongside, or in preparation for, therapeutic work.

blocks.h3: How long does it take to work?

blocks.p: You may notice small shifts within a week or two. Durable change, the kind where your baseline feels different, typically takes months of consistent, small daily practice. The timeline depends on your nervous system, your history, and your life context.

Not for basic daily practice. You probably do need additional support if you have a significant trauma history, sustained dysregulation, dissociation, or any symptoms that feel beyond your capacity to move through alone. Self-regulation practices can accomplish a lot, but at some point, you may benefit more from personal guidance.

blocks.h3: Is this the same as the vagus nerve reset?

blocks.p: No. There is no "vagus nerve reset." The vagus nerve is not broken and does not need resetting. Somatic self-regulation engages the vagus as part of a larger, ongoing practice, it does not promise to repair, reset, or unlock anything.

The broader field, polyvagal theory (Porges), somatic experiencing (Levine), sensorimotor psychotherapy (Ogden), and trauma-focused body-based approaches, has a growing evidence base. Specific practices like long-exhale breathing, orienting, and voice-based vagal engagement are supported by respiratory physiology and polyvagal research. Claims of specific, guaranteed outcomes in fixed timeframes are not.
Pick one of the three practices above. Do it tomorrow morning for thirty seconds. Do it again the morning after that.
Your nervous system already knows how to regulate. Now you practice staying out of its way and giving it what it needs.
